key_cases.case_name: South Carolina Department of Social Services v. Meek
key_cases.court: Court of Appeals of South Carolina
key_cases.holding: The court reversed the portion of an order continuing DSS custody based on the mother's conduct, holding she was entitled to notice that DSS would seek custody at the father's merits hearing, while holding that omission of the statutory boldface notices from the removal petition did not divest the family court of subject matter jurisdiction.
key_cases.relevance: It is the leading South Carolina case on the notice content of removal petitions and the effect of omitting the required warnings.
key_cases.quote: Mother's fundamental right to due process entitled her to notice that DSS intended to petition the family court for custody of the children at Father's hearing.

key_cases.case_name: South Carolina Department of Social Services v. Randy S.
key_cases.court: Court of Appeals of South Carolina
key_cases.holding: The court held that where DSS in substance removed children and placed them with a relative, it had brought a removal action and was required to follow the removal procedures — petition, 72-hour probable cause hearing, 35-day merits hearing — rather than proceeding as an intervention.
key_cases.relevance: It is the controlling authority on choosing between an intervention petition and a removal petition, and the consequences of choosing wrongly.
key_cases.quote: Despite DSS's contention that this was only an intervention action, we find the evidence supports a finding that Children were removed from Father's custody.

key_cases.case_name: South Carolina Department of Social Services v. Gamble
key_cases.court: Court of Appeals of South Carolina
key_cases.holding: The court reversed dismissal of a removal case, holding the statute requires that the merits hearing be scheduled to be held — not necessarily completed — within thirty-five days of the removal petition, and rejecting the parent's constitutional challenge.
key_cases.relevance: It answers the recurring question whether a removal case must be dismissed when the merits hearing runs past thirty-five days.
key_cases.quote: The statute requires the family court to schedule a hearing on the merits to be held within thirty-five days of the removal petition.

key_cases.case_name: South Carolina Department of Social Services v. Hogan
key_cases.court: Court of Appeals of South Carolina
key_cases.holding: The court reversed and remanded for a merits hearing, holding the family court had jurisdiction to order reunification and a merits hearing where no affirmative finding of abuse or neglect had ever been made, and condemning the practice of holding such findings in abeyance while children remain in foster care.
key_cases.relevance: It holds that a removal petition must be prosecuted to an affirmative finding under § 63-7-1660(E); agreements to 'reserve' the finding do not suffice.
key_cases.quote: We find this practice is in clear contravention of the removal statutes and could violate the fundamental right parents have to raise their children.

key_cases.case_name: Department of Social Services v. Phillips
key_cases.court: Court of Appeals of South Carolina
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed termination, holding the mother had waived objection to the removal order by not timely appealing it, that the order's placement and treatment plan satisfied § 20-7-764, and that clear and convincing evidence showed she failed to remedy the conditions causing removal.
key_cases.relevance: It sets out what the petition and resulting removal order must contain: reasons for removal, required changes, support obligations and the agency's reunification efforts.
key_cases.quote: We find the removal order sufficiently complied with the requirements set forth by section 20-7-764.

key_cases.holding: The court held that S.C. Code § 63-7-2560(A) gives every indigent parent an absolute statutory right to appointed counsel in a TPR action, including one brought privately, but affirmed termination because the erroneous denial of counsel caused no prejudice.
key_cases.relevance: Broom fixes the point at which counsel must be appointed once a termination petition is filed, whether by DSS or a private party.
key_cases.quote: S.C.Code § 63-7-2560(A) now provides an absolute statutory right to counsel for indigent parents subject to TPR proceedings
